All air and/or moisture sensitive reactions were performed under an atmosphere of dry argon using
anhydrous solvents and standard Schlenk techniques. The glassware used for such reactions was flame
dried and cooled down under vacuum then refilled with argon. Other reactions were carried out open to
air as noted in each case.
Reagents were either purchased at the highest commercial quality and used without further
purification, unless otherwise stated, or donated by our industrial collaborators.
Yields refer to chromatographically and spectroscopically (1H NMR or UPLC-MS) homogeneous
material, unless otherwise stated. Reactions were monitored by thin layer chromatography (TLC)
carried out on 0.25 mm E. Merck silica plates (60F254), using UV light as the visualizing agent and/or
panisaldehyde, KMnO4, dragendorff, DNP and heat as a developing agent or using UPLC-MS/LC-MS
analysis of a reaction aliquot. Normal phase flash silica gel chromatography was performed using E.
Merck silica gel (60, particle size 0.043 – 0.063 mm). Reversed phase purifications were carried out
NMR spectra were recorded on Bruker DRX600, DRX-500 and AMX-400 instruments and were
calibrated using residual undeuterated solvents as an internal reference (CDCl3 – 7.26 ppm 1H NMR,
77.16 ppm 13C NMR; CD3OD –  3.31 ppm 1H NMR, 49.00 ppm 13C NMR; DMSO-d6 – 2.50 ppm 1H
NMR, 39.52 ppm 13C NMR). All coupling constants (J) are reported in Hertz (Hz). Splitting patterns
are assigned as s = singlet, bs = broad singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, q = quartet, p = pentet, sx = sextet,
High-resolution mass spectra (HRMS) were recorded on an Agilent LC/MSD TOF mass
spectrometer by electrospray ionization time-of-flight (ESI-TOF) reflection experiments. The
measurements were carried out by the Automated Synthesis Facility at Scripps Research or by The
Scripps Center for Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry.
2.1 General Procedure A: Synthesis of unsubstituted sulfonyl hydrazides
The sulfonyl chloride (1.0 equiv., 20 mmol) was added to a round-bottom flask under air. The
flask was evacuated then backfilled with an inert gas 3 times (Ar or N2). Next, dry THF (30 ml) was
added, then the solution was cooled to 0 °C using an ice bath. Once at 0 °C (wait at least 10 min to
make sure it’s at 0 °C, but no more than 15 min, because it’s not stable over extended times), aqueous
hydrazine hydrate solution 50-60% [assumed 55 m/m%] (2.5 equiv., 50 mmol, 2909 mg, 2.83 ml) was
added dropwise. The formation of hydrazine hydrochloride, a white precipitate, was immediately
observed. The reaction mixture was kept at 0 °C after addition of the hydrazine until complete
consumption of the sulfonyl chloride was observed (typically < 30 min, checked by TLC 30% EtOAc
in hexanes). Note: in the unlikely case the reaction stalls, it can be warmed to room temperature.
However, these activated products can slowly hydrolyse and decompose under the reaction conditions,
thus close monitoring at room temperature is necessary.
After complete consumption of the sulfonyl chloride, EtOAc (70 ml) was added at 0 °C. The
cold reaction mixture was then transferred to a separatory funnel and washed repeatedly with brine (5
× 70 ml) in order to remove any excess hydrazine. Note: the mixture can warm up to room temperature
during workup after the addition of the organic phase, EtOAc. The organic phase was dried over
MgSO4, filtered, then evaporated, thus yielding the title sulfonyl hydrazides as a white crystalline solid
Notes: 1. The starting sulfonyl chlorides are highly crystalline solids, but sometimes supplied as orange
crystals. The 3,5-diF sulfonyl chloride can be recrystallised from hexanes (15 g sulfonyl chloride in 30
ml hexanes) using a hot filtration to remove most of the orange impurities. 2. All sulfonyl hydrazides
made during this work were obtained as white solids. In case the product’s purity in not satisfactory
(this can mainly happen due to impure sulfonyl chlorides starting materials), it can be purified by
column chromatography. In the case of the 3,5-diF sulfonyl hydrazide it was columned using 30%
EtOAc in hexanes. 3. As a precaution, the hydrazides were kept in the freezer for long-term storage.
2.2 General Procedure B: Synthesis of sulfonyl hydrazones
In a round bottom flask, the ketone (1.0 equiv., 5.0 mmol) was dissolved in dry MeOH (10 ml)
under air. Note: it’s important to completely dissolve the ketone as the product my precipitate out! Next,
the sulfonyl hydrazide (1.0 equiv., 5.0 mmol) was added in a single portion as a solid which is quickly
dissolved in the reaction mixture. The hydrazone product sometime precipitates within 5 to 30 minutes.
Note: in other cases, the product does not precipitate, please see below. The reaction mixture was
stirred for 30 min to ensure complete formation of the product, then filtered. The solid product was
washed with pentanes (3 × 35 ml), then dried under vacuum to afford the activated ketones (typically >
In case the product didn’t precipitate from the reaction mixture after full consumption of the
starting materials (usually < 30 min), the reaction mixture was evaporated to complete dryness yielding
a sticky solid/gum. Pentane (50 ml) was added and the solid was sonicated for 30 min to turn the
hydrazones into white powders. The slurry was filtered and washed with pentane (3 × 35 ml), then dried
under vacuum to afford the activated ketones (typically > 95% yield).
In case the activated ketones are not clean (because the reaction doesn’t go to competition so
there’s leftover ketone and/or hydrazide) they can be recrystallised or purified by normal and/or reverse
phase flash column chromatography. Recrystallisation was usually done by dissolving the crude in
minimal amount of EtOAc (2-3 ml), then pentane (100 ml) was added to crash out the product.
2.3 General Procedure C: Cross-coupling of sulfonyl hydrazones and (hetero)aryl
halides via in situ generated hydrazides
To a long tube a stirrer bar, the sulfonyl hydrazone (1.0 equiv., 0.50 mmol), the (hetero)aryl
halide (if solid, 1.5 equiv., 0.75 mmol), Ni(dme)Cl2 (20 mol%, 0.1 mmol, 22.0 mg), and dNH2-bpy (20
mol%, 0.1 mmol, 18.6 mg) were added. The vial was capped with a septa cap, then evacuated and
backfilled with an inert gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry DMF (2.5 ml) was added, followed by the
(hetero)aryl halide (if liquid, 1.5 equiv., 0.75 mmol), then the mixture was stirred (700 rpm) at room
temperature for 3-5 min to dissolve all the solids. Note: the colour of the mixture is dependent mostly
on the colour of the aryl halide as the nickel complex is almost colourless. Next, while stirring,
PhSiMe2H (3.0 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 204.5 mg, 230 μl) and pempidine (3.0 equiv., 1.5 mmol, 233.0 mg,
272 μl) were added. Note: there might be slight colour change to a darker shade after the addition of
the base. However, in some cases a solid is formed which is a potential indicator that the coupling will
not work due to the strong coordination of the substrate to nickel. That being said, there were coupling
reactions where a solid was formed yet we isolated the product in good yield. The reaction mixture was
again stirred at room temperature to achieve a homogenous solution (usually less than 2 min), the septa
cap was quickly replaced with a solid cap, then it was secured with a layer of electrical tape. The reaction
was transferred to a stirred (700 rpm), pre-heated oil bath at 75 °C and stirred overnight (16 to 18 hours)
at 700 rpm. Notes: 1. We highly recommend the use of a well-stirred oil bath to achieve efficient heat
transfer. Sand baths and other alternatives did not prove to be effective, because they do not reliably
heat the reaction to 75 °C. Furthermore, it is highly recommended that the level of the solvent in the
vial is below the level of the oil in the bath. 2. We do not recommend sampling the reaction before the
indicated time has passed as it can disturb the catalytic system and inadvertently quench the reaction
prematurely. 3. The reaction develops N2 gas, thus the vial becomes slightly pressurised over the course
of the reaction. The reaction mixture was transferred to a vial and the volatiles and DMF were
evaporated under reduced pressure. EtOAc (15 ml) was added, then it was washed with saturated
Rochelle’s salt solution (15 ml) to remove the inorganic salts. The phases were separated, the aqueous
phase was washed with EtOAc (2 × 10 ml), then the organic phases were combined, dried, and
evaporated to yield the crude product. Note: in case there’s a significant amount of DMF left, the crude
can be taken up in EtOAc (25 ml) and washed with 10 m/m% aqueous LiCl solution (2 × 10 ml) to
remove DMF. The crude product was purified by normal or reversed-phase column chromatography on
silica gel to give the cross-coupled product.

2.4 General procedure D: One-pot procedure for sulfonyl hydrazone synthesis
and consecutive cross-coupling with (hetero)aryl halides via in situ generated
hydrazides (One-pot of General Procedure B and C)
To a long tube the ketone (1.0 equiv., 0.5 mmol) and 3,5-difluorophenylsulfonyl hydrazide (1.0
equiv., 0.5 mmol) were added. Under air, dry MeOH (1.0 ml) was added, then the reaction was stirred
at r.t. until full conversion is observed (usually less than 30 min, the hydrazone may precipitate out,
please see above in General Procedure B). Next, MeOH is evaporated to complete dryness, thus yielding
the activated ketone which was used as described above in General Procedure C starting with adding
the other solid reagents (Ni(dme)Cl2, dNH2-bpy, and ArX).
2.5 General Procedure E: Reduction of sulfonyl hydrazones to alkyl sulfonyl
In a round bottom flask, the sulfonyl hydrazone (prepared as described above, General
Procedure B, 10 mmol) was dissolved in CH2Cl2 (25 ml) and MeOH (25 ml), then the mixture was
cooled to 0 °C. At 0 °C, NaBH4 (2.0 equiv.) was added portionwise. Note: significant H2 gas formation
was observed, hence the portionwise addition of the solid. The reaction was stirred at 0 °C for 1 h. If,
at this point, the reaction didn’t go to completion more equivalents of NaBH4 were added (1.0 equiv.
every 30 min) until complete conversion (usually stalls around 95%) was observed. Note: it is important
to keep the reaction mixture at 0 °C to suppress side-product formation. Once the reaction has reached
the desired conversion, the mixture was quenched with sat. aq. NH4Cl solution (100 ml) and the aqueous
phase was extracted with EtOAc (3 × 100 ml; alternatively, CH2Cl2 can also be used). The organic
phase was dried, evaporated thus yielding the hydrazide with sufficient purity for cross-coupling. The
hydrazides can be purified by column chromatography if necessary. Note: in our experience, many of
these hydrazides have limited stability in solution, but they are bench stable as isolated solids. So, it is

2.7 General Procedure G: Cross-coupling of alkyl hydrazides and vinyl
To a flame-dried reaction tube containing a stirrer bar, the sulfonyl hydrazide (1.0 equiv., 0.10
mmol), the vinyl halide (iodo, bromo, or triflate, if solid, 1.5 equiv., 0.15 mmol), NiCl2•DME (20 mol%,
0.02 mmol, 4.4 mg), and dNH2-bipy (20 mol%, 0.02 mmol, 3.7 mg) were added. The vial was capped
with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert gas three times. The vinyl halide (iodo,
bromo, and triflate, if liquid, 1.5 equiv., 0.15 mmol) was added, followed by dry DMF (0.5 mL), then
the mixture was stirred (600 rpm) at room temperature for 10 min to dissolve all the solids. Next, while
stirring, triethylamine (3.6 equiv., 0.36 mmol, 0.05 mL) were added. The reaction mixture was again
stirred (600 rpm) at room temperature to achieve a homogenous solution (usually less than 2 min), the
headspace of the tube was purged with a gentle stream of argon for approximately 10 seconds to remove
the air. The tube was tightly sealed, and the reaction was transferred to a stirred (600 rpm), pre-heated
oil bath at 60 °C and stirred for 3 to 12 hours at 600 rpm.
After TLC analysis showed total consumption of the sulfonyl hydrazides, the reaction was quenched
with saturated NH4Cl solution (3 mL) and extracted with diethyl ether (1.5 mL) four times. The organic
phases were combined, washed with water (10 mL), dried, and evaporated to yield the crude product.

2.8 General Procedure I: Ni-catalysed Giese-type addition of alkyl hydrazides
To a long tube a stirrer bar, the sulfonyl hydrazide (1.0 equiv., 0.2 mmol), the activated alkene (if solid,
2.0 equiv., 0.40 mmol), Ni(dme)Cl2 (20 mol%, 0.04 mmol, 8.8 mg), and dtbbpy (20 mol%, 0.04 mmol,
10.7 mg) were added. The vial was capped with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert
gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry DMF (1 ml) was added, then the mixture was stirred at room temperature
for 3-5 min to dissolve all the solids before adding Et3N (3.0 equiv., 0.6 mmol, 60.7 mg, 84 μl). The
reaction was transferred to a stirred (700 rpm), pre-heated oil bath at 75 °C and stirred overnight (12
hours) at 700 rpm. The reaction mixture was diluted with EtOAc (10 ml) and washed with sat. aq.
NaHCO3 solution (10 ml). The aqueous phase was washed with EtOAc (2 × 10 ml), the combined
organic layer was washed with brine (10 ml), dried, filtered, then evaporated to yield the crude product.
The crude product was purified by normal or reversed-phase column chromatography on silica gel to
2.9 General Procedure J: Ni-catalysed alkylation of alkyl hydrazides
To a long tube a stirrer bar, the sulfonyl hydrazide (1.5 equiv., 0.15 mmol), alkyl halide (1.0 equiv., 0.1
mmol) [in case an alkyl bromide was used, additional NaI (2.0 equiv. 0.2 mmol) was added to generate
the corresponding iodide in situ] OR redox-active ester (RAE, 1.0 equiv., 0.1 mmol), Ni(dme)Cl2 (20
mol%, 0.02 mmol, 4.4 mg), and bpp (20 mol%, 0.02 mmol, 7.2 mg) where added. The vial was capped
with a septa cap, then evacuated and backfilled with an inert gas (Ar or N2) three times. Dry DMF (0.5
ml) was added, then the mixture was stirred at room temperature for 3-5 min to dissolve all the solids
before adding Et3N (3.0 equiv., 0.3 mmol, 30.4 mg, 42 μl). Next, the cap was sealed with electrical tape.
The reaction was transferred to a stirred (700 rpm), pre-heated oil bath at 60 °C and stirred overnight
(12 hours) at 700 rpm. The reaction mixture was diluted with EtOAc (10 ml) and washed with H2O (4
ml). The organic phase was separated, the aqueous phase was extracted with EtOAc (2 × 10 ml), and
the combined organic layers were washed with brine (5 ml), dried over Na2SO4, filtered, concentrated
in vacuo, and purified by silica gel column chromatography to give the alkylated product.

Q: I am trying to prepare hydrazide from the reduction of hydrazone with NaBH4, but I am having
trouble with insufficient conversion. What should I do?
A: During the reduction of hydrazone with NaBH4, maintaining a temperature of 0°C is essential to
inhibit the formation of by-products. However, a solid is often observed forming during the reaction.
We suggest increasing the solvent volume, using more equivalent of NaBH4, and extending the reaction
time to improve conversion. If the conversion is still incomplete, purification by silica gel
chromatography and recrystallization may be required. Additionally, we found that residual hydrazone
in the crude product does not affect reactivity.
4. User guide for selecting conditions and starting materials
The user guide is presented based on currently available data separated for transformations. However,
this user guide is subject to change as more data becomes available.
1. Pempidine as the base (instead of Et3N) usually gives higher yields in the arylation protocols.
2. dNH2-bpy usually gives higher yields over dtbbpy in the arylation protocols and is more general in
terms of (hetero)aryl (pseudo)halide scope. dNH2-bpy is necessary for alkenylation and alkynylation.
3. The hydrazone arylation protocol is best suited for quick library synthesis, whereas the hydrazide
arylation protocol usually gives higher yields and affords a cleaner reaction mixture profile.
4. Et3N gives slightly higher yield in the alkenylation and alkynylation reactions.
5. ArOTf’s currently only work in the hydrazone coupling as shown in the scope. Comparing with the
corresponding hydrazide coupling, the yield drops to only around 10% (NMR). We postulate that the
decomposition rate of the hydrazide is to high, thus not matching the oxidative addition rate well in the
hydrazide coupling, whereas the hydrazone needs to be reduced which allows the coupling to occur.
6. Linear Ts hydrazides isomers are generally more stable than 3,5-difluorophenylsulfonyl hydrazides.
Both are competent in the arylation reaction and alkenylation. Linear Ts hydrazides lead to low yields
in trifluoromethylation and alkylation. In terms of alkylation, best yields are obtaining using 3,5-
